events.context: OPS-006 - learner-defined behavior matrix and expiry expectations
events.note: Learner chose the verification cases for the login slice and predicted their outcomes: 400 with one shared body for a missing or non-string email/password, one identical 401 for a wrong password and an unknown email, 401 for a missing or unknown session cookie, 200 with id/name/role for the current user, 401 for both expiry paths, and an unchanged appeals list. Predicted that an expired session is not extended (lastActivityAt stays as it was), which the mentor-run fixtures confirmed: lastActivityAt aged 31 min -> 401 with the row identical before and after, control at 29 min -> 200 with lastActivityAt advanced, createdAt aged 9 h with fresh activity -> 401 with the row untouched. One divergence found by the run: successful login answers 201 while the agreed contract says 200, which the learner aligns. Decorator spelling and expiry fixtures were mentor-supplied; the case set and the expected outcomes were the learner's.

Learner added a narrow catch around the conditional assignment update: P2025 becomes ConflictException and other errors are rethrown. API TypeScript build passed; Docker is stopped, so HTTP behavior and persistence are not yet observed.

Learner predicted the allowed assignment, forbidden client, closed appeal and missing-session outcomes before the run. Temporary fixtures then verified 200 with persisted owner/IN_PROGRESS, 403, 409 and 401; malformed id returned 400. The exact P2025 race branch remains unobserved.

Learner predicted 404 for a missing appeal and missing owner, and 400 for an existing client selected as owner. Temporary-fixture HTTP checks verified all three; rejected writes left the NEW appeal without an owner.

Learner explained that P2025 after the conditional update is a state conflict because the appeal no longer has an allowed status, while catching all errors would hide a database or infrastructure failure under a false 409. This reasoning follows the implemented narrow catch and observed matrix.

Learner created the first service-level allowed-assignment test from a worked stub example. The test instantiates the real AppealsService with a controlled repository stub and asserts the returned assignment result. Codex reran npm test (1/1 pass) and npm run build. This is assisted implementation; no independent understanding or broad skill upgrade is claimed.

Learner added a forbidden-client service test using a repository stub whose every method throws if called. The test asserts ForbiddenException with status 403, so a passing run demonstrates the early authorization path did not reach the repository. Codex reran npm test (2/2 pass) and npm run build. The implementation follows a supplied worked example and is recorded as assisted.

Learner added a deterministic service test where the repository stub passes all preconditions and only updateAppealOwner throws a real PrismaClientKnownRequestError with code P2025. The assertion observes ConflictException with status 409. Codex reran npm test (3/3 pass) and npm run build. The implementation follows a supplied worked example and is recorded as assisted.

Learner added an unexpected-error service test that asserts a generic repository error is rethrown by identity, then added a second concrete Prisma P2023 rethrow case. Codex reran npm test (5/5 pass) and npm run build. The implementation follows a supplied worked example; the additional P2023 case is code present and behavior observed, not independent reasoning evidence.

Learner repeated the taught rule that P2023 is rethrown while only conditional-update P2025 maps to 409. The response used the supplied wording, so it is recorded as assisted recognition rather than independent understanding evidence.

Learner independently explained that mapping every repository failure to 409 would falsely tell an operator there is a data-change conflict when the database may be unavailable for unrelated reasons. This demonstrates the impact of preserving unexpected errors. The relevant 5-test service matrix and build were observed.

Learner corrected an unnecessary useState hook from the static Next page and independently identified that useState becomes necessary when a component has changing local state. The final page rendered as a server component; apps/web build and lint passed, and the production server returned the Russian empty state. This is one observed frontend application, not broad Next.js mastery.
